title: Our cats episode - right here, right meow
summary: Josh and Chuck tour announcements and sponsor read open the episode, then they cover cats broadly: domestication history from the Fertile Crescent and ancient Egypt, cat anatomy (bones, tail, whiskers, detached clavicle), declawing and scratching, indoor versus outdoor cats, indoor cat care and diet, kneading, spraying, drooling, purring, catnip, and a listener email about math majors and ambiguity. Hosts share personal cat stories throughout.
topics: cats and the US Postal Service

entities.name: Stuff You Missed in History Class
Humane Society of the United States

segments.title: Tour announcements and sponsor read
segments.summary: Tour dates and ticket news for New York shows at the Bell House, plus a Squarespace sponsor read with a promo code.

segments.title: Opening banter about cats
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a cat episode and joke about their pets, nicknames, and personal preferences for cats versus dogs.

segments.title: Cat domestication history
segments.summary: Egyptians were long thought to be the first to domesticate cats, but cats lived with humans from around twelve thousand years ago in the Fertile Crescent, attracted by grain-storage rodents. Cats are technically not fully domesticated. The African wildcat is the ancestor of all house cats, and cat remains found on Cyprus suggest humans carried them there.

segments.title: Cats in the New World and indoor cats
segments.summary: Cats reached the New World, with claims tied to Columbus and early colonial ships. The false legend that Isaac Newton invented the cat flap is discussed. Keeping cats strictly indoors is a recent development, enabled by clay litter, refrigeration, and spaying and neutering. Cats were once used by the US Postal Service as paid mousers. Ed Lowe popularized clay kitty litter.

segments.title: Cat anatomy: tail, collarbone, and whiskers
segments.summary: Cats have about twenty-four bones, twenty-seven of them in the tail, which helps with balance and righting. Cats lack a collarbone, letting them squeeze through tight spaces. Cat hair has four types, and whiskers sense movement and air pressure and indicate mood. Whiskers should never be trimmed.

segments.title: Cat stuck in attic story
segments.summary: Chuck describes a time their cat, the Wizard, got trapped and panting in a hot attic, and the hosts joke about a cat curiosity mishap.

segments.title: Cat paws and declawing
segments.summary: Cat paws allow more finger-like flexing than dog paws, and claws are retractable. Declawing is compared to amputating human finger joints, and the hosts say it offers no medical benefit. Alternatives include multiple scratching posts, sticky tape, and catnip. Declawing can lead to swollen paws, biting, and loss of defense for outdoor cats.

segments.title: Indoor vs outdoor cats debate
segments.summary: Animal groups urge keeping cats indoors, citing the American Bird Conservancy estimate that US cats kill hundreds of millions of birds and over a billion small mammals yearly. Outdoor cats have a much shorter life expectancy, two to five years versus fifteen to twenty indoors. The hosts discuss humans relocating wildlife and suggest enclosed porches as a compromise.

segments.title: Caring for indoor cats and personal stories
segments.summary: Indoor cats are sedentary and prone to obesity, so they need a high-protein meat-based diet and portion control; wet food is now favored over dry. The hosts share stories of adopting their cats Lauren and Wizard, including a vet visit where Tim Curry held Lauren.

segments.title: Kneading, scent marking, spraying, and drooling
segments.summary: Kneading or making biscuits is thought to date from nursing kittens priming milk flow, and it also releases scent from paw glands for marking territory. Head-butting and facial scent glands also mark. Spraying is pungent and mostly unfixed cats do it, and drooling can signal medical problems. Cow's milk should not be fed to cats.

segments.title: Toxoplasmosis and cat litter
segments.summary: Toxoplasmosis is linked to cats and their litter, and a University of Chicago study found half of adults with intermittent explosive disorder had toxoplasmosis infections. Pregnant women should avoid litter duty.

segments.title: Purring, catnip, and cat drug culture
segments.summary: Domestic cats purr, as do some wild cats and raccoons, typically when happy but also when upset or injured. Catnip, a mint family plant, affects about half of cats, and dried or fresh leaves are both used to stimulate them.

segments.title: Listener mail on math and ambiguity
segments.summary: A listener who is a math major writes about ambiguity in math, referencing the continent naming episode and the movie Proof. Another listener, Kim, says ambiguity drove her away from math toward medical school.

segments.title: Sign-off and website plug
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners, invite contact by Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and sign off.
